name: fail-safe-defaults
intent: Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation.
problem: Authorisation written as exclusion: code asks 'is this forbidden?' and everything the deny rules do not cover - a route added last sprint, a new operation, an unknown role, an object-level case, a request the parser cannot classify - is permitted by omission. The failure modes compound it: a missing principal, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check falls through to the permissive branch, so the code paths that look most careful are the ones that open the system.
context: Any boundary where access to a resource is decided: HTTP routes and APIs, message channels and queues, object-level data access, operating-system objects and descriptors, cloud and network policy, and the configuration a product ships with. It matters most where the space of possible requests grows faster than any list of forbidden cases can track, where the check itself can fail (policy store unreachable, identity missing, input unparseable), and where an unintended permission would not be visible in normal operation.
benefits: Omission fails safe: a resource, operation or route that nobody considered is protected by construction instead of being exposed by default.
Error paths cannot grant: a missing identity, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check all end in the same deny branch instead of falling through to a permissive one.
The permission set becomes the authoritative description of what is allowed, which can be enumerated, reviewed, diffed and tested - a positive model instead of an open-ended list of exclusions.

Mistakes in the grant logic tend to over-deny, which is visible and gets fixed, rather than over-permit, which is silent and survives review and normal use (Saltzer & Schroeder's argument for permission-based decisions).
New surfaces inherit the decision: a framework-level fallback policy or a global guard protects endpoints and features added later by people who never read the security requirements.
It is what makes least privilege enforceable: the grant set is the unit that can be minimized and audited, and 'least' is meaningless while the default is 'everything'.
tradeoffs: Availability couples to the decision: failing closed means an unreachable policy source, a broken rule or a misconfigured grant denies legitimate traffic, so the system needs a deliberate degraded mode or a scoped, time-bounded, audited break-glass path instead of an implicit permissive fallback.

Denial friction has a political cost: legitimate callers hit 403s while grants are incomplete, and the fastest way to clear them is a broad grant (any authenticated user, a wildcard resource, the admin role for a service account), which recreates a permissive default at a coarser level.

Retrofitting is expensive and looks like breakage: existing permissive paths must be enumerated and granted explicitly, and long-standing implicit access - dashboards, batch jobs, internal tools - surfaces as an incident during the migration rather than as a security finding before it.

The positive model must be able to express every legitimate operation: object-level cases, ownership and delegation that the grant grammar cannot state get pushed into exception code, and exception code is where the default leaks back in.

Review and observability cost grows with the product: allow-lists accumulate entries, wildcards and generated grants, and denials that are neither logged nor distinguished ('no grant found' vs 'explicitly denied') are diagnosed slowly and widened reflexively.

participants.responsibility: The entity on whose behalf an operation is requested - user, service, process, message or job - identified by whatever credential or principal the decision point can verify.

The code that must produce a decision for every request: it looks up explicit grants and answers 'permitted' only on a match; a missing grant, an unclassifiable request or a lookup failure leaves the request denied.
The explicit positive facts - role assignments, capabilities, policy rules, ACL entries - that make access possible; nothing outside this set is permitted, which is what makes the set reviewable.
The endpoint, operation, object, topic or descriptor being accessed; it must be reachable only after the decision point has answered.
Whoever adds a grant (security owner, policy reviewer, administrator); granting is a named, reviewed act, which is what keeps the default meaningful.

use_cases: HTTP APIs and gateways: every route carries an explicit policy or permission and an endpoint whose handler was added without one is still decided (ASP.NET Core's fallback policy) or denied as unmatched (Spring Security's recommended final rule), so a forgotten decorator cannot expose it.

Message infrastructure: brokers grant publish/subscribe rights per topic, and a message whose type or destination matches no handler goes to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel instead of a catch-all consumer.

Operating-system and platform defaults: new files are created with restrictive modes (an explicit mode masked by umask, mkstemp's 0600 for temporary files, close-on-exec where descriptors cross exec), server processes run under a syscall allow-list and a least-privilege account, and firewall or network policy denies by default.

Multi-tenant data access: rows, schemas or objects are reachable only through a tenant-scoped grant, and a request with no resolvable tenant — or an unknown tenant id — is denied rather than defaulting to the shared or global dataset.

Cloud IAM and entitlement management: principals have implicit deny until a policy attaches an explicit allow, and service-to-service calls require a granted scope rather than being permitted because both ends are internal.
Product configuration and feature exposure: debug endpoints, sample data and experimental features ship disabled unless enabled, so a build cannot expose them by omission.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy default-deny: a podSelector: {} NetworkPolicy with no allowed Ingress/Egress rules isolates every pod in the namespace; allow rules are added for only the traffic that is genuinely required, making lateral movement inside the cluster the exception rather than the default.

Service mesh and mTLS (Istio, Linkerd): every workload presents a client certificate; the mesh denies any packet between workloads that cannot present a matching allowed peer identity, so compromised containers cannot reach services outside their explicit allowlist.

Policy-as-Code with Open Policy Agent (OPA) or Cedar: authorization policies are written as declarative rules in a policy language, evaluated by a purpose-built engine, and applied to APIs, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines and cloud IAM — the grant set is code, diffed and reviewed like any other artefact.

Serverless function invocation: a function's invocation permission is an explicit resource-based policy; a caller with no matching permission is denied even when the function is invoked via an authenticated event source (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), preventing unintended cross-tenant or cross-function calls.

Database row-level and column-level security: a SELECT or DML operation must match an explicit row-level policy predicate for the caller's attributes (tenant_id, role, ownership), and a missing match returns no rows rather than all rows — preventing inadvertent data leakage across security boundaries.

CI/CD pipeline permissions: a pipeline step's ability to deploy, promote artefacts or access secrets is granted through a scoped, time-bounded, revokable token; any step that has not been explicitly granted a permission is denied access to the target environment, preventing lateral movement from a compromised pipeline.

Healthcare (HIPAA minimum necessary): a clinical application's access to patient records defaults to zero; a physician's identity is matched against a role-based record access policy and granted only the specific record types (e.g. active admissions, problem list, medication history) that the physician's specialty and current assignment require — a missing match returns zero records rather than a full dataset, preventing inadvertent PHI disclosure.

Financial services (PCI-DSS): cardholder data environment access is blocked by default for all accounts; a payment processing service is granted only the specific tokenisation and authorisation operations it requires, and only for the card ranges it actively manages. A network monitoring service that has no transaction role cannot reach the cardholder data database even if it shares a subnet.

IoT device posture and network isolation: a newly provisioned IoT device ships with all external communication channels closed; it may only reach the device management plane for firmware updates and telemetry, and only over a TLS channel with certificate pinning. Any application-layer attempt to reach an external IP address is denied by a local firewall policy that is immutable post-deployment.

Multi-cloud and hybrid IAM federation: a request arriving from a federated identity (SAML assertion, OIDC token) must carry a mapped grant in the local entitlement system before accessing a resource; the federation identity alone is insufficient. A missing local grant denies even when the upstream IdP has authenticated the user, preventing an IdP compromise from automatically granting access to all federated resources.

Supply chain and CI/CD artifact access: a CI/CD pipeline stage receives a scoped, time-limited, revokable token valid only for reading the specific artifact and writing to the specific deployment target it requires; it cannot read secrets store, cannot push to the artifact registry, and cannot promote artifacts to production without a separate approval gate — following the principle that pipeline permissions are the minimum for the job, not the union of all pipeline jobs.

Runtime application self-protection (RASP): a RASP agent embedded in an application enforces default-deny at the instrumentation layer — even if an attacker achieves code execution they cannot invoke system calls, network connections or database queries that the application's normal execution profile does not require, because those capabilities are absent from the process baseline by default.

Legal and compliance data environments: an e-discovery or legal hold system defaults to zero access to case documents; a paralegal's session is granted only the specific document set for an active matter and only for the duration of that matter; a revoked matter grant cannot be exercised even if the session token has not expired, because the grant itself is checked at each document access call.

Database engine shipped defaults: PostgreSQL 15 revoked CREATE on the public schema from PUBLIC by default, inverting a default that had permitted every role to create objects since the engine's early releases — evidence that the positive model must be re-asserted in the defaults a platform ships with, not only in the application's policy.
avoid_when: The content is public by design and read-only (a documentation site, published assets): a two-zone split (published vs protected) or a small, reviewed permit-all set is simpler and more honest than a policy engine deciding nothing.
One component, one caller, one operation: a guard clause plus least privilege (separate account or process) says everything a policy layer could; the machinery would only add a thing to review.

The platform already enforces it (IAM implicit deny, database row-level security, a kernel sandbox, a managed API gateway): configure the platform and keep one source of truth, because a parallel application-level policy drifts and doubles the review burden.

A short-lived prototype or a single-tenant internal tool whose blast radius is genuinely small: a guard clause plus an explicit, written decision to revisit before exposure is the simpler answer - as long as the decision is deliberate rather than a forgotten default.
anti_patterns: Deny-list defaults: enumerating forbidden operations, so anything unlisted — including everything added later — is allowed by omission.

Fail-open error handling: catching an error from the decision and continuing (a `catch { return true; }`, a policy-service timeout treated as 'no objection', `default: allow` in the decision switch, a `rescue` that logs and proceeds).
Authentication mistaken for authorization: 'the caller is logged in' becomes the fallback grant, so every authenticated principal may do everything the system can do.
Panic grants that hollow out the default: permit-all catch-alls, wildcard resources, the admin role handed to a service account, or blanket group membership added to clear a wave of 403s.
Opt-in protection: the framework permits by default and each new endpoint must remember its guard, decorator or policy — one forgotten route is an access hole, which is the rule inverted.
Silent denials: the default-deny branch returns 403 with no log or metric, so a missing grant is indistinguishable from a broken client and the fix is to widen access.

Implicit grant through group membership: a principal is added to a broad group (all-employees, developers, internal) and inherits every permission the group carries, so removing a grant requires group restructuring rather than a targeted revocation.

TOCTOU in authorization decisions: the decision point checks a grant and returns 'permitted', but the resource's ownership or the caller's effective role changes between the check and the use, so a stale permit is honoured on an altered object.

Trusting the internal network: a service-to-service call bypasses the decision point because both endpoints are on the same VPC or cluster, recreating a perimeter-based trust instead of verifying the grant per call.

Credential-scoped overprivilege: a service account is granted the union of all permissions any of its callers might eventually need, rather than only the permission the account's own logic requires at the moment it runs.
design_principles: Fail-safe defaults (Saltzer & Schroeder, 1975): base access decisions on permission rather than exclusion - the default situation is lack of access, and the protection scheme identifies the conditions under which access is permitted.
Positive security model: state what is allowed; everything else is out of bounds, instead of trying to enumerate what is forbidden.
Least privilege: make the grant set the smallest one that supports the job; default denial is what gives 'least' its meaning.
Complete mediation: the default only binds on accesses that actually reach the decision point, so the rule presupposes an unbypassable check.
Economy of mechanism: keep the decision point and the grant set small enough to review, because the default protects only as well as the grants are understood.
best_practices: Write the deny path first: the unmatched route, the `default:` arm, the unknown operation and the missing identity all terminate in denial; the permit is the searched-for, named case.
Fail closed on every error: exception, timeout, unparseable policy, unavailable policy store and unknown role/action/tenant all deny; log and alarm instead of degrading to allow.
Wire the default at the framework level — fallback policy, global guard/filter, default-deny network policy — so surfaces added later inherit it instead of being opted in one by one.
Keep grants narrow and reviewable: no wildcards, no 'any authenticated user' where the operation is object-level, an owner and a reason per grant, and a review path for removing them.

Test the default: unknown subject, resource and action, missing metadata, policy failure and malformed input must be asserted denied, and the decision function should be fuzzed with inputs nobody anticipated.

Make denial observable and design availability deliberately: distinguish 'no grant found' from 'explicitly denied', alert on spikes, and provide a scoped, time-bounded, audited override (or a reduced-capability degraded mode) instead of a permissive fallback for outages.

Enforce fail-safe defaults at every architectural layer independently: network (default-deny firewall/NACL/security group rules), OS (syscall allow-lists, umask, seccomp), application (framework fallback policy), and data (row-level security, column permissions). Layers are complementary — one layer's bypass must not expose the asset.

Adopt Policy-as-Code and declarative Infrastructure-as-Code: express the grant set in version-controlled, reviewed, diffable policy documents (Open Policy Agent, AWS Policy, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, Terraform ACLs) so that the positive model is code and the pipeline enforces it automatically.

Align with Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207): treat every access request as if it originates from an untrusted network; verify identity and context on every call, and deny when the required grant is absent — never because both endpoints are 'internal'.

Audit the grant set continuously: scan for over-wide roles, wildcard resources, service accounts with admin grants, and inherited group memberships that silently broaden the default. Automated policy linting catches regressions before they ship.

Design a deliberate break-glass mechanism: a scoped, time-bounded, named, logged and reviewed override path — never a catch-all permissive fallback. Treat break-glass use as a security incident requiring post-event grant tightening.

Apply default-deny to new features at design time, not as a post-incident retrofit: every API endpoint, data operation, message type and infrastructure resource should have its grant model written before the handler is implemented, so the absence of a grant is the default.

Validate that the default-deny guarantee holds in federated or delegated scenarios: cross-tenant calls, service-to-service tokens and role-assertion chains must still hit the decision point and return deny when no grant matches, not because the caller's identity is trusted by virtue of being internal.

Align with CIS Benchmarks: apply the relevant consensus baseline (CIS Ubuntu, CIS Kubernetes, CIS AWS Foundations) as the starting configuration for every platform; treat benchmark deviations as security findings requiring documented justification.

Implement SOC 2 CC6.1 alignment: for new accounts, roles and service accounts the initial state must be fully restricted; a separate, reviewed, and time-limited provisioning step grants access. Automated provisioning pipelines must enforce this ordering.

Scope break-glass overrides narrowly and expire them automatically: a break-glass grant must specify the exact resource, operation, principal and time window; after expiry the grant is revoked and the incident is reviewed for permanent grant tightening — never allow an open-ended emergency override.

Separate identity verification from authorisation: a valid JWT, a successful login, or a verified service account identity is a precondition, not a grant. The decision function must still confirm that the verified principal carries an explicit grant for the requested operation before returning 'permitted'.

Design the credential scope to match the caller's own needs, not the union of all callers': a service account's permissions are the minimum required for its own logic, not for any caller that might one day invoke it — preventing a compromised service account from widening its own scope.

Validate grant grammar coverage at startup: if the policy language cannot express a required legitimate operation, surface the gap as a configuration error at startup rather than allowing the operation to fall through to the deny path silently or to be added as an exception that erodes the model.

Apply immutable infrastructure defaults: build artefacts and container images carry their own restrictive default permissions; runtime configuration cannot loosen them — only the build pipeline can produce a more permissive artefact, and that artefact is reviewed before deployment.

Enforce default-deny at the data layer: database users, row-level security policies, column permissions and API keys must start with zero access; explicit grants are added incrementally. A new database user must not be able to read any table until a reviewed grant is applied.

Integrate with Secrets Manager and Vault: credentials and tokens are fetched at runtime from a secrets manager; the decision point does not accept long-lived static credentials as evidence of a grant — each invocation proves identity freshly, following NIST SP 800-63B for authenticator lifecycle.

Apply zone-based default-deny for cyber-physical systems (CISA CPS Landscape): operational technology networks default to deny all cross-zone communications; a reviewed and tested exception list is the only permitted communication path — preventing a compromised IT endpoint from directly reaching a safety-critical PLC.
